Our editorial process produces two outputs: (i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; (ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Cnidarian hair cell development illuminates an ancient role for the class IV POU transcription factor in defining mechanoreceptor identity" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Claude Desplan as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Bernd Fritzsch (Reviewer #1); Gerhard Schlosser (Reviewer #2); Jr-Kai Yu (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) There were some possible concerns about the specificity of the POU4 antibody staining. Adding a pou4 RNA in situ either with co-staining of the POU4 antibody or a side-by-side staining will make the antibody staining significantly more trustworthy. Given that all technical aspects of this experiment are well-established, we believe that it should not be too demanding.

2) The addition of phylogenetic trees of bHLH factors that in other organisms function upstream in the regulatory cascade of pou4 (specifically the atonal/ath family) and a speculation about their possible function in the context of the nematostella hair cell type will provide interesting conceptual value to the manuscript.

3) Along the same lines, the question on the sensory modalities of these 'hair cells', including possible multimodularity, should be included in the discussion.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The study is overall very well presented and carefully discussed. I have only two comments.

First, in line 999 and following, the authors infer that the presence of a relatively large number of repressed genes in cnidocytes suggests that POU acts mainly as a repressor in these cells required to fine tune the expression levels of these target genes. But the same finding is open to alternative interpretations. The fact that is a large number of POU-IV repressed genes is expressed in cnidocytes could also mean that POU4 is not sufficient to repress these genes specifically in cnidocytes because it requires a co-repressor which is specifically absent in cnidocytes.

Second, based on morphology and some behavioral data, the authors assume throughout the manuscript that the hair cells are dedicated mechanoreceptors. However, it is equally possible that these cells are multimodal and have additional chemosensory (and/or even photosensory) functions since multimodal cells seem to be common in cnidarians. So a more careful discussion is required here. The authors should explore the transcriptome data more; maybe they provide some insight into the sensory modalities mediated by these cells.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. About the specificity of the POU-IV antibody ("Weakness" #1), I would suggest the authors to use the antigen sequence to search against the N. vectensis genome, to check whether there are any significant matches to other annotated proteins than the POU-IV factor. In addition, double staining (in situ hybridization plus immunostaining) should be helpful to verify their results.

2. As mentioned in my public review section ("Weakness" #2), the authors observed clear reduction of the phalloidin staining signals underneath the surface of the putative hair cells in pou-iv -/- polyps, however, from their EM pictures, it is not clear to me whether the rootlet structure of the apical cilium might be also affected by the loss of POU-IV function. Specifically, in their Figure 5K and 5L, the area encircled by the dotted purple line (which is really difficult to recognize!) seem to contain the structure of cilium rootlet, but it looks less prominent compared to that shown in Figure 1l. I hope the authors can provide better evidence to support their assessment on the rootlet structure phenotype.

results.result: N. vectensis hair cells have a stereotypical mechanosensory morphology with an apical cilium surrounded by eight stereovilli with actin rootlets, basal neurites, and are surrounded by support cells. Measurements of these structures are provided, and cnidocyte ciliary cones are distinguished from hair cell structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C91 provide detailed morphological characterization of hair cells using light and electron microscopy (Figure 1). The measurements are specific and the structural features are well-documented with appropriate imaging evidence. The distinction between hair cells and cnidocytes is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Hair cells are postembryonic in N. vectensis, with stereovilli first appearing at the tentacle-bud stage and not during planula development.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C94 are supported by phalloidin labeling experiments across developmental stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The temporal data clearly show the absence of stereovilli during planula stages and their appearance at tentacle-bud stage, supporting the conclusion that hair cells are postembryonic.

results.result: POU-IV protein is expressed postmitotically in nuclei of differentiating and differentiated hair cells but not in support cells in developing tentacles.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C103 are supported by immunostaining with anti-POU-IV antibody and EdU labeling (Figure 2). The antibody specificity is validated by antigen preadsorption (C101), and the postmitotic status is demonstrated by lack of EdU incorporation in >220 POU-IV-positive cells. The evidence is robust.

results.result: A pou-iv mutant allele (pou-iv-) was generated with a 705 bp deletion removing most of the POU domain and all of the homeodomain, confirmed by genotyping PCR and western blotting.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 are supported by molecular characterization including PCR genotyping (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and western blotting (Figure 3D). The deletion is precisely characterized and the mutant protein is detected at the expected size. The evidence is clear and appropriate.

results.result: pou-iv is required for touch-sensitive behavior of oral tentacles, with 100% of wildtype animals responding to touch versus only 35% of pou-iv-/- mutants, while muscle function remains intact as demonstrated by response to brine shrimp extract.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 are supported by behavioral assays with adequate sample sizes (n=44 wildtype, n=40 mutants, n=62 heterozygotes) (Figure 4). The control experiment with brine shrimp extract (C112) appropriately demonstrates that the touch insensitivity is not due to muscle defects. The behavioral phenotype is clear and well-documented.

results.result: pou-iv-/- mutants lack mature hair cells with stereovillar rootlets but retain ciliary cone-like structures, while muscles and cnidocyte precursors develop normally. Electron microscopy confirms the absence of stereovillar rootlets and cnidae in mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C122 are supported by confocal and electron microscopy (Figure 5). The sample sizes are adequate (n=6 mutants, n=6 heterozygotes, n=3 wildtype for light microscopy; n=2 each for EM). The morphological defects are clearly documented and the presence of immature hair-cell-like structures suggests a maturation defect rather than complete loss of hair cell fate.

results.result: Ciliary cone-bearing cells in pou-iv-/- mutants express mutant POU-IV protein (cytoplasmic rather than nuclear) and represent immature hair cells rather than cnidocytes, as they lack the cnidocyte marker Ncol3.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C131 are supported by immunostaining with anti-POU-IV and anti-Ncol3 antibodies (Figure 6). The cytoplasmic localization of mutant POU-IV is explained by loss of the nuclear localization signal. The distinction between immature hair cells and cnidocytes is clearly demonstrated by the absence of ciliary cones in Ncol3-positive cells.

results.result: pou-iv is not necessary for neurite extension in hair cells or cnidocytes, as immature hair cells in pou-iv-/- mutants develop morphologically normal basal neurites.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 are supported by imaging of pou-iv::kaede transgenic animals (Figure 6M-O) and Ncol3-positive cnidocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The presence of normal neurites in cells lacking functional POU-IV clearly demonstrates that neurite extension is POU-IV-independent.

results.result: POU-IV is not required for hair cell survival in tentacles, as POU-IV(-)-expressing cells in pou-iv-/- mutants do not show TUNEL-positive apoptotic nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 are supported by TUNEL assay data examining 100 POU-IV(-)-expressing cells across five primary polyps (Figure 6P-R). The sample size is adequate and the negative result is clear. This distinguishes the N. vectensis phenotype from mouse Brn-3c mutants where hair cells undergo apoptosis.

results.result: POU-IV binds to deeply conserved DNA recognition elements containing the core sequence AT(A/T)ATT(A/T)AT, nearly identical to bilaterian POU-IV-binding motifs, with preference for GC residues 5' to the core. This conservation suggests the last common ancestor of Cnidaria and Bilateria used the consensus element GCAT(A/T)ATT(A/T)AT.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C143 are supported by ChIP-seq identifying 12,972 binding sites, de novo motif discovery, comparison to Jaspar database showing significant similarity to human POU4F1/2/3 motifs (p<10^-5 to 10^-3), and EMSA validation (Figure 7). The multiple lines of evidence (ChIP-seq, motif analysis, EMSA) strongly support the conservation of POU-IV-binding motifs.

results.result: Integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data identified 4188 candidate POU-IV target genes, with 293 directly activated and 178 directly repressed. Activated genes are enriched for nervous system functions including synaptic transmission, while POU-IV negatively regulates its own expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C153 are supported by integration of ChIP-seq data with re-analysis of published RNA-seq data from NvPOU4 mutants. The criteria for target gene identification are clearly stated (ChIP peak within gene locus including promoter and gene body). GO analysis appropriately identifies functional enrichment. The finding of POU-IV self-repression is interesting and well-supported.

results.result: polycystin 1 is a POU-IV target gene specifically expressed in hair cells. The gene is 11,279 bp encoding a 3457 amino acid protein with Polycystin 1-like domain structure. POU-IV-binding motifs occur near the transcription start site, and expression is lost in pou-iv-/- mutants. This represents the first molecular marker specific to cnidarian hair cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C165 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: RNA-seq showing downregulation in mutants, in situ hybridization showing hair cell-specific expression (Figure 8A-F), RTPCR revealing the full-length transcript, ChIP-seq showing POU-IV-binding motifs at the locus (Figure 8G), transgenic reporter validation (Figure 8H-K), and loss of expression in mutants (Figure 8L-S). The phylogenetic analysis robustly places the gene in the Polycystin 1 family (Figure 8—figure supplement 2). The evidence is comprehensive and convincing.

results.result: Integration of ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and single-cell RNA-seq data identified 32 genes directly activated by POU-IV in hair cells (metacell c79), including three genes unique to hair cells. No transcription factors are activated, consistent with POU-IV functioning as a terminal selector activating effector genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C172 are supported by integration of multiple datasets. The identification of metacell c79 as the hair cell is based on unique expression of polycystin 1 components. The finding that POU-IV activates effector genes but not transcription factors in hair cells is consistent with terminal selector function. GO analysis shows appropriate enrichment for mechanosensory functions.

results.result: POU-IV activates distinct sets of genes in hair cells versus cnidocytes with no overlap, and has a greater role as a repressor in cnidocytes (81.25% of targets repressed) than in hair cells (8.6% repressed). This indicates remarkably distinct gene regulatory mechanisms in the two cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C180 are supported by integration of ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and single-cell RNA-seq data. The complete lack of overlap in activated genes between hair cells and cnidocytes is striking and well-documented. The differential proportion of repressed genes is clearly quantified and suggests different regulatory strategies. This is a key finding distinguishing the mechanisms of POU-IV function in different mechanosensory cell types.

results.result: POU-IV functions as a terminal selector of hair cell identity in N. vectensis, specifically regulating maturation but not progenitor proliferation, initial differentiation, or survival of hair cells through direct activation of cell-type-specific effector genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C187 synthesize multiple lines of evidence: postmitotic expression (C102-C103), presence of immature hair cells in mutants (C127-C131), lack of stereovillar rootlets in mutants (C116-C122), normal neurite development (C132-C133), and absence of apoptosis (C135-C136). The evidence collectively supports the conclusion that POU-IV is a terminal selector regulating maturation specifically.

results.result: POU-IV may regulate stereovillar development through activation of polycystin 1, as mouse PC-1 colocalizes with F-actin in stereovilli and regulates actin cytoskeleton organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C192 present a hypothesis based on the loss of stereovillar rootlets in pou-iv mutants and known functions of mammalian Polycystin 1. While the hypothesis is reasonable and supported by comparative data (C189-C190), direct evidence that N. vectensis Polycystin 1 regulates stereovillar structure is lacking. This requires functional analysis of polycystin 1 in N. vectensis.

results.result: Touch insensitivity in pou-iv mutants could result from defects in mechanotransduction channels. POU-IV activates mechanotransduction genes in C. elegans, and N. vectensis polycystin 1 and 2 are co-expressed in hair cells and may form a mechanosensitive complex.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C197 present alternative hypotheses for the touch insensitivity phenotype. While C196-C197 demonstrate that polycystin 2 exists and is co-expressed with polycystin 1 in hair cells, direct evidence that these proteins form a functional mechanotransduction complex in N. vectensis is lacking. The hypothesis is plausible but requires functional validation.

results.result: The role of POU-IV in mechanoreceptor development is broadly conserved across Cnidaria and Bilateria, likely predating their divergence. POU-IV is required for normal stereovillar development in both sea anemones and mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C199-C200 and C203 are supported by the findings in N. vectensis combined with extensive citations to bilaterian literature showing POU-IV function in mechanoreceptor development across vertebrates and invertebrates. The conservation of stereovillar development defects in both sea anemones (this study) and mice (Xiang et al., 1998) is particularly striking.

results.result: POU-IV has a broad role in differentiation of multiple neural cell types beyond mechanosensory cells across Cnidaria and Bilateria, suggesting ancestral involvement in multiple neural cell types. POU-IV may have controlled apical sensory apparatus formation in the last common ancestor, potentially via polycystin 1 regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C201-C202 are supported by established knowledge from multiple studies showing POU-IV function in various neural cell types. However, C204 is speculative, proposing ancestral function based on conservation in two lineages. While plausible, this evolutionary inference requires data from additional taxa to distinguish between ancestral conservation and independent evolution.

results.result: Cnidocytes have basal neurite-like processes, a finding not previously reported in cnidarian literature.
results.evaluation: Claim C210 is supported by microscopy data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I-L). This is presented as an unexpected finding. While the authors state this has not been reported previously, the novelty claim should be interpreted cautiously as absence of reports does not definitively establish novelty. Nevertheless, the observation itself is clearly documented.

results.result: Background on cnidarian phylogeny, mechanosensory cell types, and hair bundle mechanoreceptor structure in sea anemones.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C20-C21, C63-C71 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims establish the phylogenetic context and describe known features of cnidarian mechanosensory structures. The information is well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Background on N. vectensis as a model system, its development, and known features of hair bundles.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C79 provide established background on N. vectensis development and hair bundle properties, supported by appropriate citations. This contextual information is well-established in the literature.

results.result: Background on pou-iv gene in N. vectensis and validation of anti-POU-IV antibody specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 provide background from prior studies. Claim C98 validates antibody specificity by showing parallel patterns of protein and mRNA expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This is appropriate validation supporting the use of the antibody in subsequent experiments.

results.result: Background on upstream regulation of POU-IV by Atonal family transcription factors in Bilateria and presence of divergent Atonal superfamily genes in cnidarians.
results.evaluation: Claims C205-C209 provide established background on POU-IV regulation in bilaterians and note the presence of Atonal superfamily genes in cnidarians. This contextual information is well-supported by citations and sets up potential future directions for research.
